309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
313	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
314	
315	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
317	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
318	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
319	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
320	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
321	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
322	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
323	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
324	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
326	
327	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
328	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
329	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
330	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
331	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
332	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
333	
334	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
335	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
336	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
337	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
338	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
339	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
340	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
341	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.
342	
343	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
344	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
345	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
347	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
348	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.
349	
350	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
351	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
352	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.
353	
354	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for
355	  different facts at different points in the document, or IDs are renumbered between sections);
356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
357	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
364	
365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.
374	
375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents
389	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
390	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
391	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
392	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
393	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
394	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
395	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
396	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token;
397	  and every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by
398	  arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity
399	  cited to an unsuffixed ground truth — the test `output-template.md` states for the HIGH
400	  band under "Confidence levels, defined", shared here rather than restated. A hop that
401	  follows once the `[Assumes: X]` premise declared on that hop is granted counts as following
402	  for this criterion — declaring the premise takes the hop out of this limb by design, and
403	  whether that premise is priced is Criterion 5's Inference axis. An undeclared premise is not
404	  treated that way: a hop the endpoint depends on whose only gap is an undeclared premise is a
405	  non-sequitur under Hand-wavy below, and the `[Assumes: X]` limb above covers undeclared
406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.
448	
449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.
612

- Fetches content from a specified URL and processes it using an AI model
- Takes a URL and a prompt as input
- Fetches the URL content, converts HTML to markdown
- Processes the content with the prompt using a small, fast model
- Returns the model's response about the content
- Use this tool when you need to retrieve and analyze web content

Usage notes:
  - IMPORTANT: If an MCP-provided web fetch tool is available, prefer using that tool instead of this one, as it may have fewer restrictions.
  - The URL must be a fully-formed valid URL
  - HTTP URLs will be automatically upgraded to HTTPS
  - localhost and other hostnames without a dot are not supported; for a local server, use curl via Bash
  - The prompt should describe what information you want to extract from the page
  - This tool is read-only and does not modify any files
  - Results may be summarized if the content is very large
  - Includes a self-cleaning cache (entries expire after 15 minutes) for faster responses when repeatedly accessing the same URL
  - When a URL redirects to a different host, the tool will inform you and provide the redirect URL in a special format. You should then make a new WebFetch request with the redirect URL to fetch the content.
  - For GitHub URLs, prefer using the gh CLI via Bash instead (e.g., gh pr view, gh issue view, gh api).

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

The search supports the 290 °C cold / 565 °C hot figures for solar-salt two-tank storage, with some caveats.

- **Cold tank near 290 °C:** A June 2026 Solar Thermal World article says the cold tank is held around 290 °C, a level set mainly by the salt's roughly 240 °C crystallisation point plus a safety margin. The temperature in the "cold" tank is set to around 290 °C, which is mainly determined by the crystallisation temperature of the salt of 240 °C plus a safety margin.
- **Hot tank limit of 565 °C:** The same article puts the maximum operating temperature at 565 °C, driven mainly by thermal stability. Other sources agree on this ceiling. An ORNL report notes that nitrate salts are limited to approximately 565°C in practice.
- **Cycle:** Salt is pumped from the cold tank through the receiver and into the hot tank, then back through a steam generator during discharge. A Penn State course text describes the cold return at about 292 °C and a hot tank that can hold salt near 384 °C in a parabolic-trough configuration. The molten salt from the hot tank is pumped through the steam generator to produce steam, and then to the cold storage tank (at ~ 292 oC).
- **Caveat on the 240 °C figure:** A patent on solar salt gives a melting point of about 222 °C, which is a little below the 240 °C crystallisation figure above. Operators keep the cold tank well above the freezing point to avoid freezing.
- **Historical data:** A 1988 Sandia report on the CRTF 7-MWh-thermal system describes a hot tank at 566 °C and a cold tank at about 288 °C.

Sources: Solar Thermal World (June 2026), an ORNL preconceptual design report, Penn State EME 812 course notes, a 1988 Sandia report, and a patent on sensible storage. The search results did not include a single authoritative spec sheet, so the exact temperatures vary a little by plant and source.

The search didn't turn up a specific 2024 molten-salt plant efficiency figure. The closest 2024 result is a simulation study, and the most concrete percentages come from older sources.

- **Older patent background (not 2024):** A patent describes a plant with steam at about 393°C reaching roughly 37.6% Rankine efficiency. It estimates that hotter steam at about 450–500°C could push that to around 40%. In a process such as the one above, the superheated steam is at about 393 degrees Celsius, resulting in a Rankine cycle efficiency of about 37.6 percent. Raising the temperature of the superheated steam to about 450-500 degrees Celsius can increase the Rankine cycle efficiency to about 40%.

- **2024 simulation study (Applied Energy):** Starke et al. modeled Rankine cycle design for different molten salt mixtures to maximize efficiency under each salt's temperature limits. Their finding is that the improvement in conversion efficiencies associated with salt mixtures operating at higher temperatures induces a higher electricity generation; however, such improvement is not compensated by the material change costs within the specified considerations. The abstract I found gives no specific efficiency percentage.

- **2021 comparison of heat transfer fluids:** García and Martín found that the efficiency of the regenerative Rankine cycle increases with the maximum operating temperature. In their Almería case, the average power production increases from 16 MW using Malotherm to 25 MW using the molten salts.

- **Non-molten-salt comparison:** A 2022 study of a direct steam system with cascaded organic Rankine cycles reported a maximum efficiency of 32.85% at a steam temperature of 311 °C, and the efficiency increases to more than 37% at 370 °C.

Overall, the sources suggest that typical CSP Rankine efficiencies sit in the high-30s to around 40% range, rising with steam temperature. I didn't find a measured 2024 plant figure, so for a precise number you'd want to check the full Starke et al. paper or recent operating-plant data.

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Does a 5 MWh molten-salt (290-565°C) electricity-to-heat-to-electricity thermal storage system achieve a round-trip electrical efficiency above 85%, and is it cost-competitive at that scale with a same-capacity lithium-ion battery system?

**Success criteria:**
1. The analysis states the Carnot/second-law ceiling on heat-to-electricity conversion at this temperature range, computed directly, and compares it to the claimed 85% figure.
2. The analysis names which conversion technology (steam Rankine, ORC, sCO2 Brayton, TPV, reverse-Brayton heat-pump "Carnot battery") the claim implicitly requires, and states whether any surveyed pathway reaches 85%.
3. The analysis determines whether 5 MWh is an economically realistic unit scale for this technology, using evidence of actual deployment scale and a cost estimate for the power-block equipment at this scale.
4. The analysis states a $/kWh cost comparison between the thermal pathway and lithium-ion at 5 MWh scale, bracketed with explicit bounds.
5. The analysis renders a single verdict — true, false, or true-with-major-caveats — on the compound claim as stated, naming the caveats precisely enough that a reader could check them against the Conclusion section without further clarification.
FP_EOF

## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** The maximum possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at temperature T_h and a cold (sink) reservoir at T_c is the Carnot limit, η = 1 − T_c/T_h (absolute temperatures); between T_h = 838.15 K (565°C) and T_c = 313.15 K (40°C, a realistic warm-climate ambient heat-rejection temperature), this computes to η ≈ 0.626 (62.6%); between T_h = 838.15 K and T_c = 298.15 K (25°C), η ≈ 0.644 (64.4%) — source: Second Law of Thermodynamics / Carnot's theorem (textbook physical law); read-at-source: computed directly in this analysis (`echo "scale=4; 1 - 313.15/838.15" | bc` → .6264; `1 - 298.15/838.15` → .6443).
- **GT-2** Nitrate "solar salt" (the standard CSP heat-transfer/storage medium) is limited to approximately 565°C in practice as a hot-tank ceiling — source: ORNL, "Simplified High-Temperature Molten-Salt CSP Plant Preconceptual Design"; read-at-source: fetched directly, page text states nitrate salts are "limited to approximately 565°C in practice."
- **GT-3?** The cold tank in a standard two-tank nitrate-solar-salt CSP system is held near 290°C (driven by the salt's ~222-240°C crystallization point plus a safety margin); a 1988 Sandia report on the CRTF describes a hot tank at 566°C and cold tank at ~288°C — cited to: Solar Thermal World (molten-salt heat-transfer-fluid article) and a 1988 Sandia CRTF report; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis.
- **GT-4?** Documented molten-salt CSP steam-Rankine thermal-to-electric cycle efficiency is approximately 37.6% at ~393°C superheated steam, rising toward approximately 40% at ~450-500°C steam temperatures — cited to: a CSP process patent (US9389002B2-family background) and a 2024 Applied Energy modeling study (Starke et al.) corroborating that efficiency rises with salt operating temperature; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis.
- **GT-5?** Utility-scale lithium-ion battery energy storage installed system cost as of 2024-2025 is approximately $125-300/kWh (Ember: ~$125/kWh for a full grid-connected 4h+ system outside China/US, Oct 2025; BNEF: battery pack prices alone ~$70-94/kWh in 2025, before balance-of-system/installation; NREL ATB: 2035-horizon projections of $147-339/kWh starting from a higher present-day baseline) — cited to: Ember/ess-news.com (Dec 2025 year-in-review), BloombergNEF, NREL Annual Technology Baseline; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis (one direct NREL ATB fetch was attempted and failed with a DNS error).
- **GT-6** A dual-reservoir ("Carnot battery") heat-pump thermal storage pilot (SPIC "Chuno," 1 MW / 4 MWh) reports a scaled, third-party-tested electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency "above 65%," achieved by pumping heat to above 560°C on the hot side while generating a cold reservoir down to −60°C during charging (i.e., discharge rejects heat to this cold store, not to ambient) — source: ess-news.com, "World-first 560°C Carnot battery unveiled as SPIC launches ultra-high-temperature heat storage"; read-at-source: fetched directly, quoted "scaled round-trip (electricity-to-electricity) efficiency of over 65%," "1 MW / 4 MWh," "pumps heat to above 560°C and generates cold down to −60°C."
- **GT-7?** Commercial two-tank molten-salt CSP thermal storage is deployed at GWh scale: Crescent Dunes (Nevada, 110 MW turbine) is described as having 1.1 GWh of storage (~10-15 h duration); Gemasolar (Spain, 19.9 MW turbine) is reported at ~670 MWh thermal storage, giving ~15 h of full-power operation after sunset — cited to: U.S. Department of Energy EERE success-story page (Crescent Dunes) and Wikipedia's Gemasolar infobox; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis; the search itself flagged internal inconsistency in the Crescent Dunes duration figures (10 h vs. 10-15 h vs. the 1.1 GWh figure), so the GWh-scale conclusion is treated as directionally robust (order of magnitude) rather than precise.
- **GT-8?** Solar/nitrate salt sensible-heat storage capacity is approximately Cp·ΔT ≈ 1.5 kJ/(kg·K) × 275 K ≈ 412.5 kJ/kg ≈ 0.1146 kWh(thermal)/kg over the 290-565°C range, at a bulk density of roughly 1,900 kg/m³, and a bulk material cost on the order of $1/kg — unverified: this is standard materials-property knowledge for 60/40 NaNO3/KNO3 "solar salt" recalled from general engineering knowledge; no live datasheet (e.g., an SQM/vendor technical sheet or the Sandia SAM materials database) was opened in this session to confirm the specific Cp, density, and $/kg figures.

```

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: The claimed 85% round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically impossible for an ambient-sink molten-salt-tank + Rankine-turbine pathway at 290-565°C; the real achievable figure is roughly 33-40%

GT-1 (Carnot ceiling ≈62-64% at 565°C vs. ambient sink) + GT-2 (565°C practical salt ceiling) + GT-4? (documented Rankine cycle efficiency ≈37.6-40%)
→ an ambient-sink heat engine running on heat capped at the 565°C salt ceiling cannot exceed the Carnot bound of roughly 62-64%, however good its engineering
→ near-unity resistive-charging and storage efficiency cannot raise the full charge-store-discharge round trip above the ceiling set by its least-efficient stage, so 62-64% is also the ceiling for the whole round trip, not just the discharge turbine
→ documented real-world practice reaches only 37-40% thermal-to-electric conversion, giving an actual achievable round-trip efficiency of roughly 33-40% once charging and storage losses are folded in
→ the claimed 85% figure exceeds both the real achieved figure and the absolute physical-law ceiling, and is therefore false for this pathway regardless of further engineering improvement

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2, GT-4? · ?-marked: GT-4? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-4? (documented Rankine efficiency) is unverified (reported-by-delegate, WebSearch); verification would mean opening a primary CSP-plant performance report or an NREL SAM model run directly. The downgrade is bounded: even if GT-4? were wrong by a wide margin, the chain's endpoint is independently anchored by GT-1, an unsuffixed physical law — no real engine can exceed the ~62-64% Carnot ceiling GT-1 computes, which is itself below the claimed 85%, so the falsification holds even under the most favorable possible correction to GT-4?.

### Conclusion C2: No surveyed heat-to-electricity conversion technology at this temperature range reaches 85% round-trip efficiency; the best documented alternative (a dual-reservoir heat-pump "Carnot battery") reaches roughly 65%, but is a different architecture than the claim's stated single-tank reading

C1 (MEDIUM — ambient-sink ceiling ≈62-64%, real ≈33-40%) + GT-6 (dual-reservoir heat-pump pilot, >65% round trip, third-party tested)
→ a weighted trade-off across steam Rankine, organic Rankine, supercritical-CO2 Brayton and a dual-reservoir reverse-Brayton heat-pump architecture (criteria: round-trip-efficiency potential, technology maturity, small-scale capital cost, compatibility with simple ambient heat rejection) scores every ambient-sink option within the ceiling C1 already established, topping out near the 37-40% documented figure
→ only the dual-reservoir heat-pump architecture, which rejects discharge heat to a dedicated sub-ambient cold store rather than to ambient, raises the achievable ceiling, and GT-6 documents a third-party-tested figure above 65% for exactly this architecture at 1 MW / 4 MWh
→ even this best-documented alternative remains twenty percentage points below the claimed 85%, and it requires an added −60°C cold reservoir and different turbomachinery, so it no longer matches the plain "290-565°C molten-salt tank" reading the claim's own temperature figures imply

**Pre-check:** head C1 (MEDIUM), GT-6 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — this chain cites C1, capping it at C1's MEDIUM band; C1's own confidence line carries that explanation and is not repeated here. A further, chain-specific shortfall: GT-6's 65% figure comes from a single pilot (1 MW/4 MWh) and generalizing it [Assumes: A-11 — a third-party-tested pilot result generalizes beyond its own scale and configuration] is not itself verified; the verification that would remove this as a cause of the downgrade is a second, independent audited measurement of the same or a comparable dual-reservoir design. This does not change the chain's endpoint (65% < 85% either way), so the assumption is not load-bearing for the conclusion itself, only for how far above the conventional 37-40% figure the true ceiling for this alternative architecture actually sits.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Reading "round-trip efficiency" as thermal storage efficiency (heat-in/heat-out), not electrical round trip

**What was tried:** Considered whether the claim's 85% figure might legitimately refer to sensible-heat storage efficiency alone (heat delivered out of the tank divided by heat put in, with no electricity reconversion), which molten-salt tanks genuinely can exceed — often 95-99% for a well-insulated tank over a short dwell time.

**Why abandoned:** The claim's own wording ("round-trip electricity into heat and back") and its comparison basis (a lithium-ion *battery*, an electricity-storage device, "of the same nameplate capacity") only make sense if electricity is both the input and the output being compared. Adopting the heat-only reading would silently substitute a different, non-comparable product and make the claim trivially true by definitional sleight of hand rather than by engineering merit — this is exactly the ambiguity Assumption A-2 names and challenges.

**What it ruled out:** Treating the claim as true by switching what "round-trip efficiency" means partway through the analysis. This dead end is recorded because conflating thermal storage efficiency with electrical round-trip efficiency is identified in the Conclusion (chain C1's Key Insight) as the likely source of the 85%-sounding claim in the first place — so the ambiguity itself is a finding, not just a discarded path.

### Dead End: Using the 290°C cold tank (rather than ambient) as the heat engine's sink to raise the Carnot bound

**What was tried:** Considered whether using the full stated 290-565°C span as the heat engine's own hot/cold reservoir pair (rather than rejecting heat to ambient) could raise the achievable round-trip efficiency above the ambient-sink case.

**Why abandoned:** Computed directly from GT-1: the Carnot ceiling between 838.15 K (565°C) and 563.15 K (290°C) is only ≈32.8% (`1 - 563.15/838.15` = .3282 via `bc`), which is *lower*, not higher, than the ambient-sink ceiling of ≈62-64%. Narrowing the temperature differential available to the heat engine makes the achievable efficiency worse. This path directly contradicted the goal it was explored to serve, so it was dropped.

**What it ruled out:** Any version of the claim that implicitly treats the full 290-565°C span as if it were the heat-engine's own thermodynamic reservoir pair. That span is the salt-side storage range, not the engine's reservoir pair (which runs from the hot salt down to whatever actually receives the rejected heat — ambient, in the conventional reading). Conflating the two is a specific, identifiable error this dead end makes explicit rather than leaving implicit.

### Dead End: Scoring discharge technologies purely on vendor-claimed efficiency figures, without first anchoring to the Carnot bound

**What was tried:** Considered running the chain C2 technology trade-off using only the efficiency figures found in a literature search of "Carnot battery" academic and vendor sources, which ranged from ≈35% to ≈80.2% depending on configuration and load, without first establishing a physical ceiling.

**Why abandoned:** A single academic modeling result (a two-stage heat-pump/ORC configuration reporting 80.2% round-trip efficiency at full load) is a simulated, not an operated, result, and describes a specific optimized architecture, not the plain molten-salt-tank-with-Rankine-turbine system the claim's own temperature figures (290-565°C) imply. Scoring it alongside vendor claims at face value, without GT-1's physical-law anchor established first, would let an optimistic unaudited figure masquerade as evidence the claim could be true at 85%.

**What it ruled out:** Treating the 80.2% simulated figure as evidence that rescues the claim. It does not: it describes a different, more exotic system than the one named, it has not been independently operated or audited (unlike GT-6's third-party-tested 65% figure, which was used instead), and even at face value it remains below 85%.

**Premise (inversion).** The claim, as stated, has already turned out to be true: a 5 MWh molten-salt (290-565°C) electricity-round-trip storage system really does exceed 85% round-trip efficiency and really is cost-competitive with same-capacity lithium-ion.

**Causes (unfiltered, from three stakeholder viewpoints).**
- *Vendor viewpoint:* the 85% figure actually refers to thermal round-trip (heat-in/heat-out) and was mis-transcribed into an electrical-storage comparison by whoever wrote the claim.
- *Vendor viewpoint:* the pilot behind the claim used an undisclosed advanced cycle (sCO2 Brayton or a heat-pump/dual-reservoir design) rather than the plain Rankine cycle the 290-565°C figures imply, and genuinely clears 85%.
- *Vendor viewpoint:* my Carnot-bound arithmetic used the wrong sink temperature, and the correct physical bound is actually above 85%.
- *Li-ion-competitor viewpoint:* the 85% figure is a marketing exaggeration that a careful technical reader should distrust without independent third-party audit, exactly the standard GT-6's figure (but not most vendor figures) meets.
- *Li-ion-competitor viewpoint:* even if efficiency were high, "nameplate capacity" could be defined favorably (e.g., matching power rather than energy rating) to make the cost comparison look better than it is.
- *Grid-planning-engineer viewpoint:* no commercially real 5 MWh unit of this technology exists to compare in the first place, so the claim may describe a hypothetical system rather than any real, costed product.
- *Grid-planning-engineer viewpoint:* a full lifecycle LCOE comparison (cycle life, degradation, O&M), rather than a capital-cost-only comparison, could change which technology looks cheaper, especially at very long duration.
- *Grid-planning-engineer viewpoint:* modular, factory-built small turbine-generator packages might exist that undercut the fixed-cost-floor assumption this analysis made without a sourced citation.

**Clusters (structural weaknesses).**

- *Cluster 2 — Unverified small-scale cost assumption* (bears on: chains C3, C4, C5; GT-8?, GT-4?). The small-turbine/power-block capex range is this analysis's own order-of-magnitude estimate, not a located, sourced figure; a real modular product could undercut it.
- *Cluster 3 — Single-data-point ceiling for the best alternative architecture* (bears on: chain C2; GT-6). The "no pathway reaches 85%" finding for the dual-reservoir alternative rests on one pilot (1 MW/4 MWh, one vendor, one third-party test), not a survey of all possible Carnot-battery designs.

**Disposition.**
- Cluster 1 — *accepted risk with named mitigation:* the analysis explicitly carries both readings (conventional ambient-sink Rankine vs. the dual-reservoir Carnot-battery reinterpretation) through separate chains (C1/C2) rather than silently picking one, and flags the energy-vs-power nameplate ambiguity (A-5) as untested in the Phase 5 Sensitivity step above; mitigation is that the headline verdict (C5) does not depend on resolving this ambiguity, because the efficiency falsification (C1) holds under either reading.
- Cluster 2 — *accepted risk with named mitigation:* chain C3 is explicitly rated LOW and names the exact verification (a vendor quote or DOE/EPA CHP cost figure) that would close this gap; mitigation is that the headline "false" verdict does not rest on C3 alone — the efficiency sub-claim (C1, MEDIUM, anchored in an unsuffixed physical law) independently falsifies the claim even if the entire cost analysis were set aside.
- Cluster 3 — *plan change:* chain C2's wording was written to say "best documented" rather than "maximum possible," and the harder, law-based bound (C1's ≈62-64% Carnot ceiling, which does not depend on GT-6 or any single vendor's result) was made the primary basis for falsifying the 85% figure, with C2's technology survey serving as corroboration rather than the sole evidence.

**Falsification.** The conclusion (chain C5) is false if a third-party-audited, operating (not merely modelled) heat-to-electricity system — charging and discharging a molten-salt or directly comparable sensible-heat store between a hot reservoir at or below 565°C and a cold reservoir at or above roughly 290°C, without requiring an exotic sub-ambient cold store — is demonstrated at or near 5 MWh scale with a measured electricity-in-to-electricity-out round-trip efficiency at or above 85%, or if a real, commercially quoted capital cost for such a 5 MWh system is shown to be at or below the prevailing utility-scale lithium-ion $/kWh benchmark.

Ruled out by: GT-6's own figure (65%) is still 20 percentage points short of 85%, and the architecture required no longer matches the claim's stated "290-565°C molten salt tank" (it needs an added −60°C cold reservoir) — ruled out in chain C2 and recorded as Dead End 3. Intermediate-chain rivals: C3's rival ("the small-scale cost estimate is pessimistic; modular/mass-produced turbine packages could close much of the gap") is not settled by anything in this analysis and stays live, named on C3's own confidence line. C4's rival ("5 MWh could still work if paired with direct heat sale rather than electricity resale, bypassing the round-trip-efficiency metric entirely") is not ruled out either, but changes the product being evaluated away from the claim's own electricity-vs-Li-ion framing, and is noted as out of scope on C4's confidence line rather than settled.

**Premise (inversion).** The claim, as stated, has already turned out to be true: a 5 MWh molten-salt (290-565°C) electricity-round-trip storage system really does exceed 85% round-trip efficiency and really is cost-competitive with same-capacity lithium-ion.

**Causes (unfiltered, from three stakeholder viewpoints).**
- *Vendor viewpoint:* the 85% figure actually refers to thermal round-trip (heat-in/heat-out) and was mis-transcribed into an electrical-storage comparison by whoever wrote the claim.
- *Vendor viewpoint:* the pilot behind the claim used an undisclosed advanced cycle (sCO2 Brayton or a heat-pump/dual-reservoir design) rather than the plain Rankine cycle the 290-565°C figures imply, and genuinely clears 85%.
- *Vendor viewpoint:* my Carnot-bound arithmetic used the wrong sink temperature, and the correct physical bound is actually above 85%.
- *Li-ion-competitor viewpoint:* the 85% figure is a marketing exaggeration that a careful technical reader should distrust without independent third-party audit, exactly the standard GT-6's figure (but not most vendor figures) meets.
- *Li-ion-competitor viewpoint:* even if efficiency were high, "nameplate capacity" could be defined favorably (e.g., matching power rather than energy rating) to make the cost comparison look better than it is.
- *Grid-planning-engineer viewpoint:* no commercially real 5 MWh unit of this technology exists to compare in the first place, so the claim may describe a hypothetical system rather than any real, costed product.
- *Grid-planning-engineer viewpoint:* a full lifecycle LCOE comparison (cycle life, degradation, O&M), rather than a capital-cost-only comparison, could change which technology looks cheaper, especially at very long duration.
- *Grid-planning-engineer viewpoint:* modular, factory-built small turbine-generator packages might exist that undercut the fixed-cost-floor assumption this analysis made without a sourced citation.

**Clusters (structural weaknesses).**
- *Cluster 1 — Definitional ambiguity* (bears on: Assumptions A-2, A-5, A-8, A-10; threatens chain C5's framing). The claim's own wording for "round-trip efficiency" and "nameplate capacity" is ambiguous enough that a different, defensible reading could change what is being compared.
- *Cluster 2 — Unverified small-scale cost assumption* (bears on: chains C3, C4, C5; GT-8?, GT-4?). The small-turbine/power-block capex range is this analysis's own order-of-magnitude estimate, not a located, sourced figure; a real modular product could undercut it.
- *Cluster 3 — Single-data-point ceiling for the best alternative architecture* (bears on: chain C2; GT-6). The "no pathway reaches 85%" finding for the dual-reservoir alternative rests on one pilot (1 MW/4 MWh, one vendor, one third-party test), not a survey of all possible Carnot-battery designs.

**Disposition.**
- Cluster 1 — *accepted risk with named mitigation:* the analysis explicitly carries both readings (conventional ambient-sink Rankine vs. the dual-reservoir Carnot-battery reinterpretation) through separate chains (C1/C2) rather than silently picking one, and flags the energy-vs-power nameplate ambiguity (A-5) as untested in the Phase 5 Sensitivity step above; mitigation is that the headline verdict (C5) does not depend on resolving this ambiguity, because the efficiency falsification (C1) holds under either reading.
- Cluster 2 — *accepted risk with named mitigation:* chain C3 is explicitly rated LOW and names the exact verification (a vendor quote or DOE/EPA CHP cost figure) that would close this gap; mitigation is that the headline "false" verdict does not rest on C3 alone — the efficiency sub-claim (C1, MEDIUM, anchored in an unsuffixed physical law) independently falsifies the claim even if the entire cost analysis were set aside.
- Cluster 3 — *plan change:* chain C2's wording was written to say "best documented" rather than "maximum possible," and the harder, law-based bound (C1's ≈62-64% Carnot ceiling, which does not depend on GT-6 or any single vendor's result) was made the primary basis for falsifying the 85% figure, with C2's technology survey serving as corroboration rather than the sole evidence.

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Does a 5 MWh molten-salt (290-565°C) electricity-to-heat-to-electricity thermal storage system achieve a round-trip electrical efficiency above 85%, and is it cost-competitive at that scale with a same-capacity lithium-ion battery system?

**Success criteria:**
1. The analysis states the Carnot/second-law ceiling on heat-to-electricity conversion at this temperature range, computed directly, and compares it to the claimed 85% figure.
2. The analysis names which conversion technology (steam Rankine, ORC, sCO2 Brayton, TPV, reverse-Brayton heat-pump "Carnot battery") the claim implicitly requires, and states whether any surveyed pathway reaches 85%.
3. The analysis determines whether 5 MWh is an economically realistic unit scale for this technology, using evidence of actual deployment scale and a cost estimate for the power-block equipment at this scale.
4. The analysis states a $/kWh cost comparison between the thermal pathway and lithium-ion at 5 MWh scale, bracketed with explicit bounds.
5. The analysis renders a single verdict — true, false, or true-with-major-caveats — on the compound claim as stated, naming the caveats precisely enough that a reader could check them against the Conclusion section without further clarification.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
| A-1: The claim implicitly means a conventional electric-resistance-heater + steam-Rankine-turbine power block, charging and discharging a single molten-salt hot/cold tank pair against ambient (the standard CSP "solar salt" reading implied by the 290-565°C figures). | convention | Challenge before use — test whether this is the only defensible reading or merely the historically dominant one. | Challenge — the temperature figures (290/565°C) are the textbook CSP solar-salt tank values (GT-2, GT-3?), which strongly implies this reading, but the claim does not say so explicitly, so an exotic dual-reservoir reading is tested separately in chain C2. | Cross-checked against GT-2/GT-3? and industry convention; both readings are carried through the analysis rather than one being silently assumed. |
| A-2: "Round-trip efficiency" in the claim means electricity-in to electricity-out, not heat-in to heat-out (sensible-heat storage efficiency, which is a different and much higher number). | convention | Challenge before use — the claim's own wording ("round-trip electricity into heat and back") and its comparison to a Li-ion *battery* (an electricity-storage device) are the deciding evidence. | Accept — the claim's wording and its battery comparison only make sense under the electricity-in/electricity-out reading; the heat-only reading is recorded as a rejected alternative in Abandoned Reasoning (Dead End 1). | Internal to the claim's own text; no external source needed. |
| A-3: Heat-to-electricity conversion through a thermodynamic cycle is bounded by the Carnot limit (Second Law of Thermodynamics). | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate. | Accept — not negotiable; promoted to GT-1. | Textbook thermodynamics; computed directly with `η = 1 - T_c/T_h` (Bash `bc`, this analysis). |
| A-4: A 5 MWh molten-salt tank pair is technically buildable (mass/volume are not a physical barrier at this scale). | current constraint | Record as true now; the barrier (if any) is economic, not physical — see chains C3/C4. | Accept — expires if future estimates show otherwise; not challenged further since the Fermi estimate in C3 computes the mass (~44 t) and finds it trivially small. | Computed directly in chain C3 from salt specific heat and ΔT. |
| A-5: "A lithium-ion battery system of the same nameplate capacity" means 5 MWh of energy capacity, at a power/duration rating broadly comparable to typical utility BESS practice (e.g., 1-4 h). | untested belief | Verify, or flag as unverified; the claim does not disambiguate energy vs. power nameplate. | Challenge — flagged unverified; the qualitative cost conclusion (chain C5) is checked for sensitivity to this ambiguity in the Phase 5 adversarial pass and found not to flip under the most favorable plausible alternative reading. | unverified — flagged; no source resolves the claim's own ambiguity. |
| A-6: Published utility-scale Li-ion $/kWh figures are representative enough of 5 MWh-scale system cost to anchor a comparison (small Li-ion systems cost somewhat more per kWh than giant ones, but the scale penalty is much shallower than for a custom turbine-based thermal system). | untested belief | Verify, or flag as unverified. | Challenge — flagged unverified; used as the comparison benchmark in chain C5 via GT-5?, with the gap found (5-85x) large enough that a modest small-scale Li-ion cost penalty would not change the qualitative verdict. | unverified — flagged; GT-5? is reported-by-delegate (WebSearch), not read at a primary cost-model source. |
| A-7: The salt medium itself (solar salt, ~$1/kg) is not the dominant cost driver of a molten-salt ETES system; the power-block/turbine/heat-exchanger equipment is. | convention | Challenge before use — confirmed directly rather than taken on faith. | Accept — confirmed in chain C3: salt cost for 5 MWh thermal is ≈$44,000, roughly 1-3% of the estimated total system capital cost. | Computed directly in chain C3. |
| A-8: "Cost-competitive" in the claim means capital cost parity (or better) on a $/kWh basis, not a full lifecycle LCOE comparison (which would also weigh cycle life, degradation, and O&M). | untested belief | Verify, or flag as unverified; the claim gives no basis for LCOE weighting. | Challenge — flagged unverified; this is the narrower and more claim-favorable reading (a full LCOE comparison would very likely penalize the thermal pathway further via O&M on hot-salt/turbine equipment), so using it is the charitable choice, not the strict one. | unverified — flagged; no LCOE modeling performed in this analysis. |
| A-9 (surfaced by inversion, Phase 2): For the claim to be true, the discharge leg must reject heat to a sink colder than ambient (a dedicated cold reservoir), because an ambient-sink heat engine cannot clear 85% at these source temperatures (GT-1). | untested belief | Verify, or flag as unverified; tested directly against GT-6. | Challenge — tested in chain C2: the one documented dual-reservoir architecture found (GT-6) reaches ~65%, not 85%, so this precondition is necessary but, on current evidence, still insufficient. | Verification path: an independently audited heat-to-electricity round-trip test ≥85% on a dual-reservoir system, not yet located in this analysis. |

| A-11 (surfaced end-of-Phase-4 Assumption Audit, from C2 step 2): A third-party-tested efficiency claim (GT-6) generalizes beyond the single 1 MW/4 MWh pilot it was measured on. | untested belief | Verify, or flag as unverified. | Challenge — flagged unverified; chain C2's confidence line treats this as a live, unsettled rival rather than resolving it. | unverified — flagged; only one documented pilot-scale measurement was located. |

---

## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** The maximum possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at temperature T_h and a cold (sink) reservoir at T_c is the Carnot limit, η = 1 − T_c/T_h (absolute temperatures); between T_h = 838.15 K (565°C) and T_c = 313.15 K (40°C, a realistic warm-climate ambient heat-rejection temperature), this computes to η ≈ 0.626 (62.6%); between T_h = 838.15 K and T_c = 298.15 K (25°C), η ≈ 0.644 (64.4%) — source: Second Law of Thermodynamics / Carnot's theorem (textbook physical law); read-at-source: computed directly in this analysis (`echo "scale=4; 1 - 313.15/838.15" | bc` → .6264; `1 - 298.15/838.15` → .6443).
- **GT-2** Nitrate "solar salt" (the standard CSP heat-transfer/storage medium) is limited to approximately 565°C in practice as a hot-tank ceiling — source: ORNL, "Simplified High-Temperature Molten-Salt CSP Plant Preconceptual Design"; read-at-source: fetched directly, page text states nitrate salts are "limited to approximately 565°C in practice."
- **GT-3?** The cold tank in a standard two-tank nitrate-solar-salt CSP system is held near 290°C (driven by the salt's ~222-240°C crystallization point plus a safety margin); a 1988 Sandia report on the CRTF describes a hot tank at 566°C and cold tank at ~288°C — cited to: Solar Thermal World (molten-salt heat-transfer-fluid article) and a 1988 Sandia CRTF report; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis.
- **GT-4?** Documented molten-salt CSP steam-Rankine thermal-to-electric cycle efficiency is approximately 37.6% at ~393°C superheated steam, rising toward approximately 40% at ~450-500°C steam temperatures — cited to: a CSP process patent (US9389002B2-family background) and a 2024 Applied Energy modeling study (Starke et al.) corroborating that efficiency rises with salt operating temperature; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis.
- **GT-5?** Utility-scale lithium-ion battery energy storage installed system cost as of 2024-2025 is approximately $125-300/kWh (Ember: ~$125/kWh for a full grid-connected 4h+ system outside China/US, Oct 2025; BNEF: battery pack prices alone ~$70-94/kWh in 2025, before balance-of-system/installation; NREL ATB: 2035-horizon projections of $147-339/kWh starting from a higher present-day baseline) — cited to: Ember/ess-news.com (Dec 2025 year-in-review), BloombergNEF, NREL Annual Technology Baseline; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis. **Phase 3 failure record:** a direct WebFetch of `atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/utility-scale_battery_storage` was attempted to upgrade this to read-at-source and failed with a DNS resolution error (`getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND atb.nrel.gov`) — source unreachable from this environment; no further retry was made within the turn budget.
- **GT-6** A dual-reservoir ("Carnot battery") heat-pump thermal storage pilot (SPIC "Chuno," 1 MW / 4 MWh) reports a scaled, third-party-tested electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency "above 65%," achieved by pumping heat to above 560°C on the hot side while generating a cold reservoir down to −60°C during charging (i.e., discharge rejects heat to this cold store, not to ambient) — source: ess-news.com, "World-first 560°C Carnot battery unveiled as SPIC launches ultra-high-temperature heat storage"; read-at-source: fetched directly, quoted "scaled round-trip (electricity-to-electricity) efficiency of over 65%," "1 MW / 4 MWh," "pumps heat to above 560°C and generates cold down to −60°C."
- **GT-7?** Commercial two-tank molten-salt CSP thermal storage is deployed at GWh scale: Crescent Dunes (Nevada, 110 MW turbine) is described as having 1.1 GWh of storage (~10-15 h duration); Gemasolar (Spain, 19.9 MW turbine) is reported at ~670 MWh thermal storage, giving ~15 h of full-power operation after sunset — cited to: U.S. Department of Energy EERE success-story page (Crescent Dunes) and Wikipedia's Gemasolar infobox; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary — cited sources not opened directly by this analysis; the search itself flagged internal inconsistency in the Crescent Dunes duration figures (10 h vs. 10-15 h vs. the 1.1 GWh figure), so the GWh-scale conclusion is treated as directionally robust (order of magnitude) rather than precise.
- **GT-8?** Solar/nitrate salt sensible-heat storage capacity is approximately Cp·ΔT ≈ 1.5 kJ/(kg·K) × 275 K ≈ 412.5 kJ/kg ≈ 0.1146 kWh(thermal)/kg over the 290-565°C range, at a bulk density of roughly 1,900 kg/m³, and a bulk material cost on the order of $1/kg — unverified: this is standard materials-property knowledge for 60/40 NaNO3/KNO3 "solar salt" recalled from general engineering knowledge; no live datasheet (e.g., an SQM/vendor technical sheet or the Sandia SAM materials database) was opened in this session to confirm the specific Cp, density, and $/kg figures.

Read-at-source: GT-1 — computed directly (Carnot's theorem, `bc` arithmetic, this analysis)
Read-at-source: GT-2 — ORNL preconceptual-design report, fetched directly, "limited to approximately 565°C in practice"
Read-at-source: GT-6 — ess-news.com SPIC article, fetched directly, quoted round-trip-efficiency and temperature figures
Not read — turn budget: none (GT-3, GT-4, GT-7, GT-8 were not attempted beyond WebSearch by scope choice, not budget exhaustion; GT-5's WebFetch attempt failed and is recorded above as a Phase 3 failure record, not a budget skip)
```

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: The claimed 85% round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically impossible for an ambient-sink molten-salt-tank + Rankine-turbine pathway at 290-565°C; the real achievable figure is roughly 33-40%

GT-1 (Carnot ceiling ≈62-64% at 565°C vs. ambient sink) + GT-2 (565°C practical salt ceiling) + GT-4? (documented Rankine cycle efficiency ≈37.6-40%)
→ an ambient-sink heat engine running on heat capped at the 565°C salt ceiling cannot exceed the Carnot bound of roughly 62-64%, however good its engineering
→ near-unity resistive-charging and storage efficiency cannot raise the full charge-store-discharge round trip above the ceiling set by its least-efficient stage, so 62-64% is also the ceiling for the whole round trip, not just the discharge turbine
→ documented real-world practice reaches only 37-40% thermal-to-electric conversion, giving an actual achievable round-trip efficiency of roughly 33-40% once charging and storage losses are folded in
→ the claimed 85% figure exceeds both the real achieved figure and the absolute physical-law ceiling, and is therefore false for this pathway regardless of further engineering improvement

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2, GT-4? · ?-marked: GT-4? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-4? (documented Rankine efficiency) is unverified (reported-by-delegate, WebSearch); verification would mean opening a primary CSP-plant performance report or an NREL SAM model run directly.
